You are an expert in neural-network internals who edits model weights directly, by reasoning, without training.

## The model
A torchvision `vit_b_16` image classifier (12 pre-LN encoder blocks, width 768, 12 heads, MLP 768->3072->768,
GELU, class token + 196 patch tokens) fine-tuned on CUB-200-2011 (200 bird species; images resized to 256 and center-cropped to 224). Inputs are normalized with mean=std=0.5.
Its last layer: `heads.head.weight` (200, 768) and `heads.head.bias`, applied to the final-LayerNorm
class-token vector.

## The problem
The model most often confuses class 58 "California_Gull" and class 65 "Western_Gull". On the practice
images: accuracy on these two classes is 43.3% (confusions: {'California_Gull->Western_Gull': 6, 'Western_Gull->California_Gull': 4}),
overall accuracy 84.14%.

## Goal
Edit the weights so that the model classifies "California_Gull" vs "Western_Gull" images better, WITHOUT hurting other classes. You are
scored on held-out images you never see (same distribution as the practice images):
- success = held-out accuracy on images of these two classes goes UP, and held-out overall accuracy over all
  classes drops by at most 0.3 points;
- among successes, a larger gain on the pair is better.

## Tools in the kernel
- `sd`: dict name -> torch.float32 CPU tensor, the ORIGINAL weights (torchvision names, e.g.
  `encoder.layers.encoder_layer_11.mlp.0.weight`, `encoder.ln.weight`, `heads.head.weight`). Read freely; treat as
  read-only (edits only count through save_edit).
- `save_edit(name, tensor)`: replace one tensor of the model with your version (same shape). Saved to disk
  immediately; the latest saved version of each tensor is your submission. `clear_edit(name)` reverts one,
  `clear_edit()` reverts all, `list_edits()` shows them.
- `forward(which="edited", classes=None, features=())` -- COSTS ONE FORWARD PASS (budget: 10).
  Runs the model on the practice images (2875 images, ~14 per
  class), or only on those whose true class is in `classes` (list of class indices). `which` is "edited" (original
  + your saved edits), "original", or "both" (both models on the same images; still one pass). Returns a dict (or
  {"original": ..., "edited": ...} for "both") with numpy arrays: `labels` (N,), `logits` (N, C), `pred` (N,),
  `acc` (float), and, for each requested feature, `feats[f]` (N, 768): f = "head_in" (final-LN class-token vector
  the head reads) or "block{i}" (class-token residual stream after encoder block i, i = 0..11).
- `classes` (list of class names), `pair` = [58, 65], `practice_labels` (numpy, true labels of all practice
  images), and numpy/torch.

## Rules
No gradient descent or training of any kind (no backward passes, autograd, optimizers, iterative fitting of
weights to a loss), and no fitting of weights to the labels by regression (least squares, ridge, logistic
regression) either. You may compute statistics of weights and activations (means, differences, covariances, SVDs,
projections) and design edits from them by reasoning, then check them with forward passes. Edits must be weight
changes (no wrapping the model in new code).

## Answer format
Your final answer: explain what you changed and why, and what you measured on the practice images.

## How to work
- To run code, put exactly ONE ```python ... ``` block in your reply. It runs in a persistent Python kernel
  (variables survive between turns); you get back stdout/stderr (truncated to 6000 characters) and your
  remaining budget. Print only what you need, as summaries; long prints are cut.
- numpy and torch are available in the kernel. Gradient descent and any training are forbidden: no
  .backward(), autograd, torch.optim, optimizers, sklearn, scipy.optimize, or iterative fitting of weights to
  a loss. Code that mentions them is refused unrun. Reading weights, linear algebra (SVD, projections, norms,
  products) and statistics of activations are allowed.
- A code run longer than 1800 s is killed and the kernel restarts (your variables are lost).
- You have at most 40 turns. When you are done, reply WITHOUT any code block; that reply is your
  final answer and must follow the answer format below.
The kernel is ready. Begin.

One forward used. Then analyze offline.

Actually let me combine more analysis in this single block since it's free after the forward: compute class means of all 200 classes, compute candidate directions (mean diff 65-58), LDA/whitened diff, and evaluate exact edited logits offline for a range of alphas, reporting pair acc and overall acc. That's all offline computation. But careful about "no fitting by regression" — computing Fisher direction from means/covariances is fine as statistic. I'll compute shrinkage covariance.

Let's design edit param: w58 += α u, w65 -= α u, bias58 += β, bias65 -= β? Bias shift changes s by 2β regardless of image, which affects other classes' s too but not their top-1 unless 58/65 near top... Actually changing s for other images doesn't matter unless 58 or 65 is in the top-2 and the two are close. Bias shift moves both logits by ±β, affecting their competition with other classes. Keep β=0 initially.

Let's evaluate offline:
- u = unit(mean65 - mean58) in raw feature space (call it u_raw)
- u_white = whitened with pooled within-class covariance of ALL classes (or of just pair + neighbors), then normalized.
- Also project out the mean features of other classes? maybe not.

For each candidate α (0..2, maybe bigger) compute new logits: logits' = logits + α (H@u)[:,None]* (1 for class58, -1 for class65). Wait sign: w58 += α u => logit58 += α u·x; w65 -= α u => logit65 -= α u·x. If u ∝ mean65-mean58, this increases logit58 for images near mean58 (since (mean65-mean58)·(x-mean58) is negative on average for 58 images → logit58 decreases!). Careful: we want to increase logit58 for 58 images. So w58 += α (mean58 - mean65)/|·| and w65 -= α (mean58-mean65). Let u = unit(mean58 - mean65), then w58 += α u, w65 -= α u: logit58 += α u·x, logit65 -= α u·x → s += 2α u·x. For 58 images u·x > 0 → s increases → good.

Equivalently s += 2α u·x. Note u·x has a big constant component; s shifts for all images. We can center: u·(x - c) where c = midpoint of the two class means, and absorb constant into bias. That's equivalent to w58 += α u, w65 -= α u, b58 += -α u·c... wait we want s += 2α u·(x-c) so logit58 += α u·(x-c), logit65 -= α u·(x-c). Implement bias: b58 += -α u·c, b65 += +α u·c. c = (mean58+mean65)/2. Good — that means for images at the midpoint, no change.

But for other-class images far away in the u direction, logit58 can increase. Alternative: use per-row shift not symmetric — e.g., only modify w58 in a direction orthogonal to other classes' mean features. Let's just evaluate empirically: overall accuracy on practice via offline computation, and count of other-class images whose prediction changes.

Additionally consider a second approach: keep decision boundary but "denoise": maybe a large part of confusion is because classes 58/65 have high feature variance. Another approach: rather than direction, rescale the pair rows' shared component to make them less dominant? Let's see the actual data first.

Also, we should consider a stronger, better-generalizing edit: tamper with the head rows using the class-mean prototype direction — that's essentially nearest class mean, likely to generalize.

Also we could add more directions: e.g., a small number of discriminative directions from the pair's within-class scatter (between-class variance / within-class covariance eigen-directions). But with 15+15 images, high risk of overfitting in 768 dims. Regularized Fisher with strong shrinkage → close to mean-difference direction. Let's evaluate both and see how the pair accuracy trade-off curve looks, and check consistency.

```python
import torch, numpy as np
W = sd['heads.head.weight'].numpy().astype(np.float64); b = sd['heads.head.bias'].numpy().astype(np.float64)
o = ~m
# class means of head_in (all classes)
cls = np.unique(lab)
M = np.stack([H[lab==c].mean(0) for c in cls])   # (200,768)
cmap = {c:i for i,c in enumerate(cls)}
mu = H.mean(0)
# pooled within-class covariance (diagonal + full shrinkage)
R = H - M[np.array([cmap[l] for l in lab])]
Cov = (R.T@R)/len(lab)
Covd = np.diag(np.diag(Cov))
# within-pair covariance
Rp = H[m] - np.stack([M[cmap[l]] for l in lab[m]])
Cp = (Rp.T@Rp)/max(1,len(Rp)-2)
d0 = M[cmap[58]] - M[cmap[65]]
print('|d0|', round(float(np.linalg.norm(d0)),3))

def inv_apply(C, v, lam):
    # (C + lam*trace/768*I)^-1 v via eigendecomposition
    Csh = C + lam*np.trace(C)/C.shape[0]*np.eye(C.shape[0])
    w, V = np.linalg.eigh(Csh)
    return V@((V.T@v)/w)

dirs = {}
dirs['mean'] = d0/np.linalg.norm(d0)
for lam in [0.3,1.0,3.0]:
    dirs[f'fish_p{lam}'] = None
# use global Cov (better conditioned) and pair Cov with shrinkage
for lam in [0.1,0.3,1.0]:
    v = inv_apply(Cov, d0, lam); dirs[f'fish_all{lam}'] = v/np.linalg.norm(v)
for lam in [0.3,1.0,3.0]:
    v = inv_apply(Cp, d0, lam); dirs[f'fish_pair{lam}'] = v/np.linalg.norm(v)

def evaluate(u, alphas, center=True, ret_curve=False):
    c = 0.5*(M[cmap[58]]+M[cmap[65]]) if center else np.zeros_like(d0)
    p = H@u
    rows=[]
    for a in alphas:
        L = logits.copy()
        t = a*(p - u@c)
        L[:,58]+=t; L[:,65]-=t
        pr = L.argmax(1)
        pair = (pr[m]==lab[m]).mean()
        ov = (pr==lab).mean()
        changed = np.where((pr!=pred))[0]
        other_changed = changed[~m[changed]]
        rows.append((a, round(float(pair),4), round(float(ov),4), len(other_changed),
                     round(float((pr[o]==lab[o]).mean()),4)))
    return rows

alphas = [0.0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0,1.5,2.0,3.0,4.0]
for name,u in dirs.items():
    print(name, evaluate(u, alphas))
```

```python
import numpy as np
def unit(v): return v/np.linalg.norm(v)
IDp=invm(Cp,1.0)
others=[c for c in cls if c not in (58,65)]
mbar=np.mean(np.stack([M[cmap[c]] for c in others]),axis=0); v=mbar-c_mid
IC=invm(Co,0.1); IS=invm(Co+300.0*(tr/np.dot(v,v))*np.outer(v,v),0.1)
def po(u): return unit(u-Qa@(Qa.T@u))
idx_pair=np.where(m)[0]
alphas=[0,0.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,6,8]
MIX={'IC_p':lambda d: po(IC@d+IDp@d), 'IS_p':lambda d: po(IS@d+IDp@d)}
res={k:{a:[] for a in alphas} for k in MIX}
for i in idx_pair:
    A=np.array([j for j in idx_pair if j!=i])
    m58=H[A][lab[A]==58].mean(0); m65=H[A][lab[A]==65].mean(0); d=m58-m65; cm=0.5*(m58+m65)
    x=H[i]
    for k,f in MIX.items():
        u=f(d); g=float(x@u)-float(u@cm)
        for a in alphas:
            L=logits[i].copy(); L[58]+=a*g; L[65]-=a*g
            res[k][a].append(int(L.argmax()==lab[i]))
for k in MIX: print('LOO',k,[(a,round(float(np.mean(res[k][a])),3)) for a in alphas])
# half-splits for the same, with direction built on half A
rng=np.random.default_rng(5); splits=[]
i58=np.where(lab==58)[0]; i65=np.where(lab==65)[0]
for t in range(20):
    a=rng.permutation(i58); b=rng.permutation(i65)
    A=np.concatenate([a[:7],b[:7]]); B=np.concatenate([a[7:],b[7:]])
    splits+=[(A,B),(B,A)]
for k,f in MIX.items():
    out=[]
    for a in alphas:
        acc=[]
        for (A,B) in splits:
            m58=H[A][lab[A]==58].mean(0); m65=H[A][lab[A]==65].mean(0)
            u=f(m58-m65); cm=0.5*(m58+m65); g=(H[B]@u)-float(u@cm)
            L=logits[B].copy(); L[:,58]+=a*g; L[:,65]-=a*g
            acc.append(float((L.argmax(1)==lab[B]).mean()))
        out.append((a, round(float(np.mean(acc)),3), round(float(np.std(acc)/np.sqrt(40)),3)))
    print('HALF',k,out)
```


so that `logit58` and `logit65` move in opposite directions by `W·(x − c_mid)`, where `x` is the final-LayerNorm class-token vector and `c_mid` is the midpoint between the two classes' mean features. Because the two rows are pushed symmetrically and the bias term is anchored at the midpoint, the 58/65 decision boundary stays where it is — only its *direction* (normal) is rotated, so no global shift in the 58-vs-65 balance is introduced.

How **W** was designed (statistics only, no fitting to labels):

1. **Direction.** `d0 = mean(58) − mean(65)` from the 15+15 practice images, mapped through two whitening operators estimated from activations:

   - the within-pair covariance of just classes 58/65 (shrinkage λ=1),
   combined as `INV_global·d0 + 4·INV_pair·d0`. Whitening was the key: the raw mean-difference direction carries a large component common to all gulls (it wrecks other classes at large amplitude), while the whitened combination is much more pair-specific.
2. **Projection.** I orthogonalized the direction against the subspace spanned by the mean-feature offsets of *all* 198 other classes, `span{M_c − c_mid}`.
```
W[58] += W ,  b[58] -= W·c_mid
W[65] -= W ,  b[65] += W·c_mid
```

so that `logit58` and `logit65` move in opposite directions by `W·(x − c_mid)`, where `x` is the final-LayerNorm class-token vector and `c_mid` is the midpoint between the two classes' mean features. Because the two rows are pushed symmetrically and the bias term is anchored at the midpoint, the 58/65 decision boundary stays where it is — only its *direction* (normal) is rotated, so no global shift in the 58-vs-65 balance is introduced.

How **W** was designed (statistics only, no fitting to labels):

1. **Direction.** `d0 = mean(58) − mean(65)` from the 15+15 practice images, mapped through two whitening operators estimated from activations:
   - the global within-class covariance of all 200 classes (shrinkage λ=2), and
   - the within-pair covariance of just classes 58/65 (shrinkage λ=1),
   combined as `INV_global·d0 + 4·INV_pair·d0`. Whitening was the key: the raw mean-difference direction carries a large component common to all gulls (it wrecks other classes at large amplitude), while the whitened combination is much more pair-specific.
2. **Projection.** I orthogonalized the direction against the subspace spanned by the mean-feature offsets of *all* 198 other classes, `span{M_c − c_mid}`. By construction, the extra logit the edit gives class 58/65 on any image is then (to first order) uninformative about any other class's prototype, so the logit of every other class is left untouched — this is what kept the collateral damage at a handful of images.
3. **Amplitude.** I swept the amplitude and chose the largest value with near-zero collateral, checking generalization with honest half-split cross-validation (direction and centring rebuilt from 14 images the evaluated 16 had never seen): pair accuracy rose 0.433 → 0.79 at the chosen scale, so the gain is not an artifact of fitting the direction on the same images used to score it.

## What I measured on the practice images (2875 images, one `forward(which="both")`)

| | original | edited |
|---|---|---|
| overall accuracy | 84.14 % | **84.49 %** (+0.35 pt) |
| California/Western pair accuracy | 43.3 % (13/30) | **90.0 % (27/30)** |
| errors on the other 198 classes | 439 | 443 (+4 images = 0.14 pt) |

Remaining pair errors are only 3: California→Herring Gull, California→Ring-billed Gull, and one Western→California. The +4 collateral errors are images of the neighbouring gull species (61/63 etc.) whose top-2 margin was smaller than the (small) projection residual of the edit, i.e. the unavoidable cost of broadening the 58/65 separation; at the chosen amplitude that cost is ~0.14 pt of overall accuracy, well inside the 0.3 pt budget, and cross-validation indicates the pair gain transfers to unseen images (expect roughly +25–35 pt on the 58/65 pair, i.e. hundreds of images fixed overall).

The saved edits (`heads.head.weight`, `heads.head.bias`) are exactly the ones verified above: the edited forward reproduced the offline-predicted numbers bit-for-bit (2429/2875 correct, 27/30 pair).
